title: Inquest into death in Pentciton jail cell begins
article: A man who died in the Penticton RCMP lock-up two years ago, repeatedly banged on his cell door while asking to be taken to hospital, a coroner's inquest was told.

Steven Joseph Scott, 30, died in the early morning hours of Aug. 12, 2012. He had been taken into custody the previous morning in an intoxicated state outside a home on Killarney Street where he had formerly resided.
A coroner's inquest into the death opened Monday in Penticton court before Coroner Larry Marzinzik and a five-member jury.
Originally placed in the drunk tank, Scott was later transferred to a regular cell prior to an afternoon appearance before a justice of the peace.

RCMP Const. Ryan Shedden testified that Scott mentioned he suffered from low blood sugar and suggested he might need to be taken to hospital at some point. However, he said was all right for the moment and indicated medications weren't required.

John Cairn, who was occupying a nearby cell at the time, testified by phone from Ontario that he was awoken in the middle of the night by the sound of Scott kicking and banging repeatedly on his cell door. Scott claimed he was having trouble breathing and needed medical attention.

However, Cairn said cell guards and police officers rejected the prisoner's pleas to be taken to hospital. Scott complained about similar problems during a previous weekend in jail and had been transported to hospital for treatment.
Cairn said guards or police officers did come into the cell block in an attempt to calm Scott down.
"I recall them saying that he's not getting out of doing another weekend (in custody)," Cairn said. "From what I heard, I was disgusted. I actually yelled at them: 'Get him some freaking help.'"

Cairn said he later urged Scott to try to putting his arms up over his head in order to breathe better. After a while, his protests and banging became fainter. Fellow inmates assumed he had eventually fallen asleep.
Despite the guard doing regular cell checks by video and in-person, Scott wasn't discovered to be dead until later in the morning, several hours after an autopsy determined he had died.
Shedden said he entered the cell at 10:40 a.m. and saw Scott lying on his cell bench.
"He was in a fetal position facing the wall. He was all covered with a blanket except for his feet," the police officer testified.
Attempting to rouse him, Shedden discovered the man's body was cold and stiff, and his feet had turned purple.
Jail guard Neil Eshleman, who came on duty shortly before 6 a.m., said although Scott hadn't touched his breakfast, that was a common occurrence among prisoners who sleep in.

Eshleman said it is very difficult to determine by video or by looking through a cell window whether a prisoner is breathing. However, he agreed in hindsight, he should have noticed that Scott had never moved from his position.
RCMP policy states that guards are not allowed to enter a jail cell on their own and must call in an RCMP member on duty.

The inquest is scheduled to continue today and Wednesday, hearing from 19 witnesses before the jury will begin its deliberations. A coroner's inquest does not involve any criminal charges, but the jury can make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future.
